# The Politics of Language and the Limits of Words

There is a telling inconsistency in how the media handled the language of the Vietnam War. Official military terminology was quoted directly and without challenge, its euphemisms and abstractions absorbed into news reports as though they were neutral facts. Yet when it came to acts of protest—Stephen Smith's burning of his draft card, or Norman Morrison's self-immolation—the same reporters reached for quotation marks, a subtle signal of distance and skepticism. The gestures of dissenters were framed as suspect, held at arm's length, while the sanitized vocabulary of those waging the war was allowed to pass unexamined.

Norman Morrison was a Quaker from Baltimore. In November 1965, he protested the war in Vietnam in the most absolute way a person can: he burned himself to death. He did so not with any specialized apparatus but with ordinary household materials, an act whose very simplicity underscored its gravity. Here was a man who had turned the commonplace objects of domestic life into the instruments of a final, unbearable statement.

The reaction of the press was immediate and revealing. Reporters set out at once to explain his death as the product of mental illness, to file it away under the reassuring category of individual derangement. But they found no evidence to support that story. Morrison had not been unstable; there was no pathology to point to, no breakdown that would allow his act to be dismissed and contained.

Part of what unsettled the journalists was the sheer silence of what he had done. Morrison offered no advance warning, issued no press release, left behind no tidy, quotable statement to slot into a headline. There was nothing for the photographers to anticipate and nothing for the writers to paraphrase. Confronted with an act that refused to package itself for the news cycle, they were left unprepared and hesitant, unsure how to report something that would not translate into their familiar formulas.

And this, finally, is the author's point. Morrison's protest was wordless, but it was not without meaning. His silent, bodily act of self-sacrifice communicated something more powerful and more complete than any statement delivered by officials such as Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara. Where their words obscured and abstracted, his body spoke with a terrible clarity. The language of policy could be quoted endlessly and still say nothing; a single, deliberate death said everything.
outputs.L4:
# Three Acts of Burning

The poem draws its power from a deceptively simple structure: it places three separate acts of burning side by side and asks the reader to weigh them against one another. Each act involves fire, and each involves destruction, yet the way society records, frames, and responds to them could not be more different. By juxtaposing these events, the poem forces us to confront an uncomfortable question about how we assign meaning and moral weight to violence.

The first act is small and personal. Stephen Smith burns his draft card—a single sheet of paper set alight as an act of conscience and refusal. In the eyes of the law and the media, this is a punishable transgression, an offense worthy of coverage and condemnation. A young man's gesture of defiance is catalogued, quoted, and treated as a matter of public concern, as though the burning of paper were among the gravest threats to the social order.

The second act is vast and institutional. Robert McNamara, as an architect of military policy, presides over the bombing of those officially designated "Enemy Aggressors." Here the poem's use of quotation is pointed and ironic: the very phrase "Enemy Aggressors" is a piece of official language, a bureaucratic euphemism that transforms the incineration of human beings into a sanctioned, even noble, act of state. This burning—incomparably larger in its human cost—is not condemned but justified, wrapped in the vocabulary of policy and defense. The media that scrutinizes a single draft card treats the mass violence of war as an abstraction, its horror dissolved into strategic rhetoric.

The third act is the poem's moral center. Norman Morrison, a Quaker, sets himself on fire in an act of self-immolation, offering his own body as a protest against the war. His death is silent; he makes no speech, issues no press release, quotes no official phrase. And yet, the poem suggests, his wordless sacrifice communicates a truth more profound than any of the carefully framed language surrounding the other two burnings. Where McNamara's violence hides behind euphemism and Smith's small act is amplified into scandal, Morrison's gift of his own life stands outside the machinery of quotation and coverage altogether.

Through repetition and irony, the poem exposes the moral disparities embedded in how we speak about death and destruction. The same word—*burning*—applies to all three acts, but language and media distribute blame, sympathy, and significance in ways that have little to do with actual human suffering. A card is protected; a napalmed village is rationalized; a man's self-sacrifice is nearly lost in silence. By setting these acts in stark parallel, the poem indicts a society that has learned to validate institutional violence while criminalizing dissent and overlooking the very sacrifices that speak most truthfully to conscience.

In the end, the poem argues that meaning cannot be measured by the volume of coverage or the authority of official rhetoric. Morrison's silence outweighs McNamara's justifications precisely because it asks nothing and claims nothing except the terrible sincerity of a life freely given. The truth, the poem insists, is not always the loudest voice—sometimes it is the one that burns without a word.

# Stephen Smith: A University Journey

Stephen Smith had always dreamed of attending university. From a young age, he understood that higher education could open doors to opportunities that would otherwise remain closed. When the acceptance letter finally arrived, marking his admission to the University of his choice, Stephen felt a wave of excitement and pride wash over him.

## The Early Days

Stephen's first weeks at university were both thrilling and challenging. The sprawling campus, with its historic buildings and modern facilities, initially felt overwhelming. However, Stephen quickly adapted to his new environment. He explored the library, joined student societies, and began building friendships that would last a lifetime.

The transition from high school to university life required significant adjustment. Stephen learned to manage his own schedule, balance coursework with social activities, and take responsibility for his own learning. These skills would prove invaluable throughout his academic career.

## Academic Pursuits

At university, Stephen chose to study a subject he was passionate about. His professors challenged him to think critically and question assumptions. The Smith family had always valued education, and Stephen was determined to make them proud.

Late nights in the library became routine as Stephen tackled complex assignments and prepared for examinations. Though the workload was demanding, he found genuine satisfaction in mastering difficult concepts and expanding his knowledge.

## Growth and Discovery

University offered Stephen more than just academic learning. He discovered new perspectives, encountered diverse cultures, and developed a deeper understanding of himself and the world around him. Through debates, discussions, and collaborative projects, Stephen grew into a more confident and capable individual.

## Looking Forward

As Stephen Smith progressed through his university years, he began thinking about his future career. The education and experiences he gained would serve as a foundation for whatever path he chose to pursue. His time at university represented not just an academic achievement, but a transformative chapter in his personal development.

For Stephen, university was more than an institution—it was where he discovered his potential and prepared to make his mark on the world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem addressed to Robert McNamara about Norman Morrison, the Quaker who set himself on fire in 1965 to protest the Vietnam War.
counterfactuals.output:
**To Robert McNamara, on the Man Beneath Your Window**

Mr. Secretary, do you remember November,
the second day, the failing light,
when a man walked toward the Pentagon
carrying his daughter and a can of kerosene?

You were counting somewhere in that building—
tonnages, tallies, the arithmetic of war,
the elegant graphs of what a nation could sustain—
when Norman Morrison set down the child

and set himself alight beneath your window.
Emily lived. Someone took her from his arms
before the flame. That much mercy he permitted.
The rest he gave entirely to the fire.

He was a Quaker. He believed in the small
inextinguishable light inside a person,
and having seen your war burn children
he chose to burn a witness back at you.

You wrote of it, years after, in your book:
you said it moved you, said you locked the grief away,
could not speak of it even at your own table,
the horror sealed behind your careful face.

I do not write to damn you. I write to ask
what a man is worth against a machine of state,
and whether one deliberate human fire
can reach the window of a reasonable heart.

He thought it could. He staked his flesh upon it.
And you went on. The graphs went on. The war
consumed its arithmetic of years and dead.
But something crossed your window that November—

a light you carried, by your own admission,
down all the quiet corridors of age:
the man who would not let you not remember,
who signed his conscience in a script of flame.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an anti-war prose poem that contrasts the burning of a draft card, the self-immolation of Norman Morrison, and the bombing of Vietnamese villages, using repetition and bitter irony directed at a government official.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Fire Knows

*Mr. Secretary, there are three fires I would speak of.*

---

The first fire is small. It fits in the cupped palm of a boy who has decided that his hands are his own. He touches the flame to a little rectangle of paper, a number, a name, a sorting-code that said: *you belong to the machine.* The card curls. The card blackens. The card becomes a gray feather that lifts on the wind and is gone.

*Mr. Secretary, they arrested him for this. For the small fire. For the paper. You called it a crime against the nation, this boy who burned only what belonged to him. Remember that. Remember what you called a crime.*

---

The second fire is larger. It is a man named Norman Morrison, thirty-one years old, standing below your window with his daughter in his arms and gasoline in his hands. He set the child down first — remember that, he set the child down — and then he became the thing he could not stop seeing. He became the burning. He made of his own body a candle held up to your window so that you could not say you had not seen.

*Mr. Secretary, you saw. You wrote later that you saw. You went home to your family and you did not speak of it, you said, because it was too painful. Remember that word. Painful. Remember whose pain silenced whose dinner table.*

---

The third fire is enormous. It does not fit in a palm or below a window. It falls from the bellies of aircraft in canisters that bloom into orange gardens across the villages of a country most of the burned could not find on your maps. It is jelly that sticks to skin and keeps its burning. It is the roof of the house, the roof of the school, the roof of the child who was set down by no one, held by no one, seen by no one with a window to jump beneath.

*Mr. Secretary, this fire you did not call a crime. This fire you called policy. This fire you called necessary, measured, proportionate, regrettable. Remember your words. Remember which fires needed no arrest.*

---

So let us be clear about the arithmetic of flame.

The boy burned paper — and was a criminal.
The man burned himself — and was a tragedy you kept from your children.
The state burned villages — and was a government doing its solemn duty.

*Mr. Secretary, the fire knows the difference between these three, even if you do not. The fire that ate the draft card and the fire that ate Norman Morrison and the fire that ate the village — they are all the same fire, and it has been asking you a question by its light, the same question, all these years:*

*What did you see from your window?*
*What did you see?*
*What did you burn to keep from seeing?*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece in the style of 1960s protest poetry that critiques the media's silence around Norman Morrison's self-immolation outside the Pentagon.
counterfactuals.output:
**Silence Below the Wall**

They tell you nothing of the man
who walked to the river of the Pentagon
with his daughter on his hip
and gasoline for a prayer.

November, and the leaves already down,
the ink already dry
on the morning's approved edition—
*no room, no room, the presses hum,
we lead with weather, war by inches,
a senator's clean shoe.*

Norman Morrison,
who folded himself into flame
beneath the window of the men
who count the dead by category,
who filed him under *incident*,
who spelled his fire in a single column
buried past the box scores.

Where were your cameras, gentlemen,
when the light he made
lit up the granite face of the machine?
You who chase a burning barn,
a burning car,
a burning house on a slow news Tuesday—
you looked away from a burning conscience
because it asked a question
your advertisers would not sponsor.

He did not shout.
He did not need to.
The fire said everything,
and you—
you turned the volume down,
you paraphrased the smoke,
you interviewed the pavement
and forgot to ask the ash
what it had been.

They sang his name in Hanoi.
They named a street.
And here, in the country he was burning for,
the anchors cleared their throats
and moved along, moved along,
the story sponsored by the soap
that gets your linens whiter
than a folded flag.

Remember the arithmetic:
one man, one match,
against the long division of a war—
and the papers that could not spare
an inch of honest black
to say he lived, he chose, he meant it.

So print this where they won't:
that silence is a kind of gasoline,
that turning the page
is a kind of striking match,
and every morning we say nothing
we agree to let the burning go on
behind the wall,
below the fold,
out of the frame,
where the powerful prefer their fires kept.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

kept their cool and abstract distance.

burned what he said was himself,
and I ask you now, across the years:

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a searing political poem about language, silence, and moral witness, referencing Stephen Smith burning his draft card and Norman Morrison's protest against the Vietnam War.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Fire Said**

There are words, and then there is what
the mouth cannot hold—the way a nation
learns to say *defense* and mean *the burning*,
to say *containment* and mean the child in the field.

Stephen Smith struck a match to paper
and the small flame ate his name from the ledger of the state.
A card is only card until it means
your body given over, your consent inscribed
in the actuary's neat, indifferent hand.
He would not sign. He would not lend his silence
to the arithmetic of other men's decisions.
Watch how a single fire can un-write
what a thousand pens have sworn.

And Norman Morrison, beneath the Pentagon window,
in the failing light of November,
set his daughter down—gently, gently,
that was the whole argument, that gesture—
and became the sentence no one could redact.

Because language had gone hollow.
Because *escalation* is a word that does not scream.
Because the reports came clean and typed and bloodless
while the villages burned in a grammar no one printed.
He answered with the only text left uncensored:
the flesh, the flame, the terrible legibility of a man
refusing to look away from what he'd seen.

We are taught that silence is a kind of safety,
that to say nothing is to owe nothing.
But there is a silence that is complicity's quiet cousin,
that sits in warm rooms while the maps are colored red,
and there is a silence *after*—
the one that follows witness,
the hush in which the whole world, for one moment,
is made to read.

They will tell you the poem changes nothing,
that fire is only fire, that a burned card
grows back in triplicate.
Maybe. But the moral witness does not act
to win. He acts because the alternative
is to let the language do its quiet murder,
to let *acceptable losses* pass the lips
like weather, like the price of tin.

So remember the ones who would not be fluent
in the tongue of their times—
who took the smooth official word
and held it to the flame until it screamed
what it had always, secretly, meant.

Remember that conscience, when all else is bought,
still keeps one thing it can spend:
the body, and its stubborn, burning *no.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
